study.title: Proverbs 23 Prudence before pleasure, money, discipline and wine
study.overview: Proverbs 23 gathers practical warnings about four areas in which the human heart easily deviates: the table of power, ambition for wealth, the moral formation of children and the domination of appetite, especially in alcohol. The chapter does not just deal with external behavior; it insists that desires, memories, thoughts, and expectations must be governed by the wisdom and fear of the Lord. In the whole section, wisdom appears as an active choice: to observe, restrain, listen, receive discipline, value the truth and reject what enslaves.

outline.title: At the table of the ruler: self-control and detachment
outline.explanation: The first verses warn against the seduction of refined food and social opportunity before a domineer. The table can hide interest and trap, and prudence has to limit appetite and not make wealth the supreme target of life.

outline.title: Discernment in relations, justice and formation of the heart
outline.explanation: The section combines warnings against false hospitality, against injustice with orphans, and in favour of discipline. He also teaches that the joy of parents is linked to the wise way of children and that the fear of the LORD must replace the envy of sinners.

outline.title: Right way, honor parents and value of truth
outline.explanation: Here the sage is called to listen, avoid destructive companies and honor father and mother. Truth, wisdom, discipline, and prudence are portrayed as something to be acquired and preserved, because they bring joy to the family and confirm a just legacy.

outline.title: Danger of immorality and drunkenness
outline.explanation: The last part puts side by side the sexual seduction and the seduction of wine. Both lead to pain, loss of control, moral insensitivity and ruin. The chapter ends with the tragic image of the drunkard who suffers, does not perceive and still desires to repeat the same sin.

study.context: The chapter reflects wisdom instructions to everyday life, especially for young people in formation. The notes highlight concrete situations: meals in the presence of a ruler, desire for wealth, unfair practices against the fragile, correction of children, coexistence with drunkards and the appeal of prostitution. The scenario is that of the common social and family life, in which wisdom needs to be applied with attention, self-control and fear of God.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that the human heart is not neutral: it is attracted by pleasure, gain, social approval and drunkenness. Biblical wisdom does not condemn food, wealth or joy itself; it condemns the disorderly use of these things as the ultimate end. The fear of the LORD appears as the decisive reference that relativizes the prosperity of sinners and sustains the hope of the righteous. The conviction also arises that God defends the vulnerable, especially the orphans, and judges injustice. The discipline, including the correction of children, is presented as a means of preserving life, not as cruelty. Finally, the chapter shows that sin promises freedom, but surrenders slavery, shame and insensitivity.

scholarViews.insight: The first warning applies to young people in service before a ruler: the abundance of the table can seduce excess, making the inexperienced vulnerable due to lack of self-control.
Wealth can also be an idol; the warning is not to make enrichment the main goal of life, for this makes the heart as trapped as the gluttony.
The reference to the "redentor" of the orphans points to someone who defends their cause with justice; in the case of the text, God takes this cause and vindicates it.

questions: In what situations are you most tempted to lose your own domain: on the table, in money, in the approval of others or in hidden pleasure?
How can the instruction to value truth, discipline and prudence change concrete decisions in their family and professional routine?
What practices can you take to admire the success of sinners, but to maintain the fear of the Lord as the main criterion?
study.practice: Choose an area of vulnerability and practice a concrete act of wisdom this week: eating more moderation, reviewing a financial goal, seeking reconciliation with parents or guardians, or cutting off a situation that favors sin. It is also worth making a practical commitment to study and keep the truth, rather than just listening to it. The chapter calls a life of containment, obedience and continuous vigilance, not of impulse.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow you to identify some interpretive readings, but do not solve all the translation and direction options in detail. In particular, in 23:11 the figure of the "redentor" can be understood more directly as a defender of the cause of the orphans, without requiring a technical definition beyond what the notes affirm. There is also no support for broad historical reconstructions in the notes; therefore, the study is limited to what the text and the commentators provided support.
